Tuairisc Bhainistíochta Mhíosúil an Príomhfheidhmeannach – 31ú Lunasa 2025 
Chief Executive’s Monthly Management Report – 31st August 2025 
 
 
 
A Chara, 
 
I enclose the above report for your statutory consideration, this report has also been prepared under Section 136 
& 138 of the Local Government Act, 2001. The attached report is the Chief Executive’s Monthly Management 
Report for August 2025, detailing activities, updates, and progress across various departments of Louth County 
Council.  
 
Below is a summary of the key highlights: 
 
1. Finance and System Support 
• 
Expenditure: €106.85M spent (58% of the 2025 budget). 
• 
Income: €110.54M collected (60% of the 2025 budget). 
• 
Debtors: Total outstanding balance of €46.86M. 
• 
The process for Budget 2026 has commenced and the Council vote note to increase in Local Property Tax 
(LPT) for 2026. 
• 
The ICT Department dealt with 898 support call which 91% have been resolved. 
 
2. Economic Delivery 
• 
Tourism: Louth and Meath secured €100,000 annually for three years under the "Home of Halloween" 
strategy. 
• 
Shopfront Improvement Grant: 30 applications received to date. 
• 
Boyne Valley Flavours: New website development and ongoing initiatives to promote local food culture. 
• 
The Night-Time Economy: hosted a number of events to engage a more vibrant nighttime economy. 
• 
Heritage Week: largest ever Heritage Week took place, with more than 50 separate events taking place 
across the county, as well as dozens of open days. 
 
3. Operations and Environment 
• 
Road Maintenance: an very extensive road repairs, drainage works, and litter management across the county 
continue. 
• 
Illegal Dumping: CCTV installed at three sites and  194 investigations completed in August. 
• 
Climate Action: Progress on the CLIMAAX risk project and Community Climate Action Fund projects. 
• 
Annual Mattress and Couch Amnesty anti-dumping initiate has commenced. 
• 
Solar Photo Voltaic Project is still ongoing 
• 
Digital Hub: commencing as planned  
• 
Renovation of Drogheda Cornmarket buildings: continuing at place. 
 
4. Housing and Culture 
• 
Homelessness: 160 adults in emergency accommodation; 27 families with dependent children. 
• 
Housing Allocations: 73 units allocated in August. 
• 
Housing List: 5,033 applicants on the housing list. 
• 
Energy Efficiency Retrofits: 138 units targeted for 2025. 
• 
Cultural Services:  
o 
Libraries hosted 1,090 children for the Summer Stars Reading Programme; 
o 
Libraries hosted celebrated local history as part of heritage week. 
o 
Arts: Culture Night 2025 launched with events across the county.

Museum: New exhibitions featuring African art and sporting memorabilia. 
• 
Creative Ireland: Biodiversity mural completed in Blackrock Community Park. 
 
 
5. Major Capital Projects 
• 
Westgate Vision (Drogheda): Planning documents finalized for urban regeneration. 
• 
St. Nicholas Quarter (Dundalk): Phase 1 nearing substantial completion; Phase 2 in design. 
• 
Narrow Water Bridge: Construction progressing, with bridge fabrication ongoing in Belgium.

Greenways: Carlingford Lough Greenway completed; Dundalk Bay to Carlingford Greenway in design. 
• 
Active Travel 
• 
€6.3M allocated for 28 projects promoting walking and cycling infrastructure. 
•

initiatives.

• In August 2025 Customer Services dealt with 16,419 queries inclusive of 7,968 calls, 1,250 e-mails and 
7,201 counter queries. 10,174 (62%) of queries received were dealt with at first point of contact.: 
• Age-Friendly Projects: Ardee Garden Care and Repair Project showcased to the Age-Friendly Judging 
Panel. 
• Ukraine Response: Summer camps and outdoor activities organized for Ukrainian families. 
• Healthy Louth: Ran the following in August, Irish Homeless league, promoting dog fouling awareness, 
breastfeeding-friendly spaces, and female participation in sports. 
 
These highlights provide an overview of the key activities and achievements in Louth County Council for August 
2025.  
 
I would like to especially thank all the executive and staff of LCC for their work and commitment, which is outlined 
in more detail in the attached report.

Cyber Security 
The ICT Department provide regular cyber security training to all staff within the organisation. The theme of the 
training in August emphasised how USB drives pose cybersecurity risks as they can carry malware or 
ransomware that infects systems when plugged in, and they can also be easily lost or stolen, leading to data 
breaches. Staff were reminded to remain vigilant by only using authorised devices, avoiding unknown USBs, 
and reporting any suspicious activity to IT security teams.

Lú Festival of Light  
The ‘Ireland, Home of Halloween’ Strategy aims to 
position Ireland as the authentic global home of 
Halloween.  Following a competitive process, Louth 
and Meath County Council have been successful in 
their application to funding under the Fáilte Ireland 
pilot scheme ‘Home of Halloween’.  Under the 
scheme Louth and Meath will receive up to €100,000

This investment will support the development of 
vibrant Halloween experiences that attract visitors 
during the off-peak season and contribute to 
regional economic growth.  Lú Festival of Light is the 
named project for Co. Louth.  Staff within the Council 
have joined the steering committee for Lú Festival of 
Light which is being delivered in 2025 by Love 
Drogheda BIDS.

Drogheda Code Campaign Workshop 
 
Context: Toward the end of July key stakeholders 
participated in a workshop to develop a campaign to 
address anti-social behaviour and promote a safe 
culture of care in Drogheda’s nightlife.  
 
Case Study: Inspired by the Bristol Rules 
campaign, a collaborative initiative between Bristol 
City Council, universities, and local venues aimed at 
promoting safe and respectful behaviour in the night-
time economy; this approach was selected by the 
Drogheda Purple Flag working group. 
 
Participants: 
Community-minded 
stakeholders 
from diverse backgrounds, chosen for their

positive night-time environment.

Encouraging 
sensible

Ensuring respect for everyone, including

Walled Towns Day events funding 
In addition to and related to Heritage Week, the Irish 
Walled Towns Network (the IWTN), a programme of 
the Heritage Council, has approved funding for 
public celebratory events, ‘Walled Towns Festivals’, 
to take place in early to mid-September, in both 
Carlingford and Drogheda. 
 
The Drogheda Walled Town Collective will stage the 
Seán Corcoran Series from Friday 5th to Sunday 7th 
September.  The Heritage Office is also supporting 
this festival.

Carlingford

IWTN conservation funding 
The Irish Walled Towns Network also provides 
funding for conservation works, including for 
research and studies to make future conservation 
works possible.  The IWTN has offered funding of 
€30,000 for the creation of a detailed conservation 
and interpretation plan for a long stretch of 
Drogheda’s town wall at Featherbed Lane.  This 
project is currently on eTenders, and subject to

first week of September.

Research Enquiries 
The preservation of archives is a vital need for our 
society and the service receives a steady volume of 
enquiries on archives. Research enquiries include 
those from private individuals, academics (historians, 
archaeologists, social scientists, etc), professionals 
(solicitors, engineers, planning consultants, etc), 
family historians, students and state agencies. The 
Archivist also supports staff in various sections with 
many business-related enquiries.   
A collection recently used for research was the 
County Committee of Agriculture and Technical 
Instruction, set up in 1901 when Louth County 
Council adopted the Agricultural and Technical 
Instruction Acts 1889-1899.  In addition to 
departmental funding, the Acts gave councils the 
power to levy rates to finance the committees, which 
provided technical instruction through various 
schemes and encouraged rural industry.  
 
Such schemes included horticulture, butter making, 
poultry keeping, soft fruit growing, food production 
schemes, the breeding of horses, cattle, or pigs, 
agricultural shows and local exhibitions.  This was the 
start of the vocational education system. The 
Technical Instruction Committee was replaced in 
1930 by the County Louth VEC that was set up under 
the Vocational Education Act, while the County 
Committee of Agriculture continued until a new semi-
state training and advisory organisation called ACOT 
(An Chomhairle Oiliúna Talamhaíochta – Council for 
Development in Agriculture) was established for 
farmers in the early 1980s, which was subsequently 
replaced by Teagasc. 
 
The County Committee of Agriculture archive 
collection held in Louth County Archives consists

mainly of minute books from 1901 – 1985 and annual 
reports from 1939 – 1986. The collection provides a 
valuable insight for researchers into agricultural 
education and changes in agricultural practices in 
Louth over the course of the twentieth century.
